newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Giant Russian plants say Ukraine alumina ties sour.
newsitem.headline: Giant Russian plants say Ukraine alumina ties sour.

text.p: A war of words between giant Russian aluminium smelters and a big raw materials supplier in Ukraine blew up on Thursday as relations between the two sides appeared to deteriorate.

The world's two largest aluminium smelters, Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk, both in Siberia, said the Mykolayiv alumina plant in southern Ukraine was charging too much for its alumina, a raw material the smelters need to import to make refined aluminium.

"Unfortunately we cannot agree on the price, and their (Mykolayiv's) price is higher than world prices," Yuri Shlaifshtein, a board member at the world's largest aluminium smelter Bratsk, told Reuters.
Mykolayiv denied the charge, saying the aluminium producers were using strongarm tactics to make it drop its prices.

"All of these comments are being made with the goal of influencing our actions and forcing us to sell our product at a lower price," said Valery Agafonov, financial director of Mykolayivskiy Hlynozemny Zavod, in the south of Ukraine.
Agafonov denied that Mykolayiv was charging above world prices.
The aluminium producers said they would look for alumina suppliers outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
"We say now we will buy alumina outside the CIS. There it is much cheaper," said Gennady Druzhinin, board chairman at Krasnoyarsk, the world's second biggest plant.
Despite rising tension in talks between the two sides, neither said it wanted to cut ties altogether.
Shlaifshtein said Bratsk intended to return to the negotiating table in March.
Agafonov agreed: "We are prepared to continue to work with Russian aluminium smelters in 1997, especially since our plant produces 20 percent of the alumina that Russia needs."
Mykolayiv plans to produce one million tonnes of alumina this year, enough to make around 500,000 tonnes of aluminium. It traditionally supplies 90 percent of its output to Russia.

Russia, which produced 2.87 million tonnes of aluminium in 1996, relies heavily on alumina imports, and has been seeking supply contracts from the Mykolayiv plant with an eye to securing nearby raw materials at low prices.
Both Bratsk and Kransonyarsk said that they have covered most of their alumina requirements for 1997, although some purchases still need to be made.
In 1996 Bratsk produced 783,000 tonnes of refined aluminium and Krasnoyarsk 777,000 tonnes.
"We still have some shortfalls. Out of around 1.5 million tonnes of alumina (for 1997), we still need 30,000 to 40,000 tonnes," Krasnoyarsk's Druzhinin said.
"We have basically covered our needs (for 1997)," Bratsk's Shlaifshtein added.
Druzhinin said the breakdown in discussions between the two sides was costing his plant money.
"We are losing money, because abroad the price of alumina is rising," he added.
Prices firmed lately to around $185/190 a tonne, fob Australia, from $140/145 in the third quarter last year, Macquarie Equities said in a recent report.
